1037.title: Al-Aqsa in Jerusalem
1037.hook: the farthest mosque in Jerusalem, named third in the hadith of the three mosques
1037.howItsDone: Muslims who can travel to Jerusalem often pray at al-Aqsa, and those who cannot remember it in their prayers and in the story of the Night Journey, recited from Surah al-Isra.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Prophet's Mosque in Medina, raised beside his home, where he now rests near the Rawdah. Your line was his mosque.

On a wide stone platform in the Old City of Jerusalem, two buildings catch the light. One wears a golden dome: the Dome of the Rock, a shrine built over the rock, which we met months back. The other is lower and longer, at the southern end, under a plainer gray dome. The gold steals the eye. But the long building is where the rows form on a Friday, shoulder to shoulder, facing south toward Mecca. Its name comes straight out of a verse of the Qur'an. Today: Al-Aqsa in Jerusalem.
screen: `ONE PLATFORM, TWO BUILDINGS.` → `THE GOLD DOME IS THE SHRINE.` → `THE ROWS FORM AT THE FAR END.`

segments.voice: Start with the verse. Surah seventeen opens with the Night Journey of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. In Pickthall's translation, God carried His servant by night "from the Inviolable Place of Worship to the Far Distant Place of Worship." The Inviolable one is the mosque in Mecca. The Far Distant one, in Arabic al-masjid al-aqsa, is the farthest mosque, and the verse gave the place its name. Notice what it leaves out: it never names Jerusalem. Muslims have understood the Far Distant place as the mosque there. Second, the list from two days ago. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says not to set out on a special journey except to three mosques: the Sacred Mosque in Mecca, the Prophet's own mosque in Medina, and al-Aqsa. Jerusalem is named third, and this week has walked them in that order. Third, an older link. In another hadith, a companion, Abu Dharr, asked which mosque was set up first on earth. The answer: the Sacred Mosque. And then? Al-Aqsa. The two are paired from the start. Fourth, the name stretches. Some use al-Aqsa for the long prayer hall alone; others for the whole walled enclosure, courtyards, trees, the Dome of the Rock and all, also called the Noble Sanctuary. The same hill is holy to Jews, who call it the Temple Mount, and the city is dear to Christians. A crowded holiness, and a reason people of more than one faith pray for its peace.

segments.voice: Hold Jerusalem in mind as a place, not a headline: stone streets, bells and calls to prayer, families buying bread, children on their way to school, worshippers of more than one faith passing in the same lanes. If you pray, ask in your own words for peace and safety for the city and everyone who lives there; if you don't, simply wish them well, one face at a time.
Al-Aqsa, the farthest mosque named in the Qur'an's verse of the Night Journey, and third in the hadith of the three mosques. Today's word.
Your line: the farthest mosque. Named in a verse, and paired with Mecca from the start. Day one thousand thirty-seven, done.

1038.title: Mosques of mud and wood
1038.hook: Djenné in Mali, wooden mosques in China and Java
1038.howItsDone: Muslims pray in mosques of every style and material, and when no mosque is near they pray on any clean ground or a prayer mat, facing the direction of Mecca.

segments.voice: Yesterday: al-Aqsa, the Far Distant Place of Worship in Jerusalem. Your line was the farthest mosque.

Three roofs. The first is flat, on walls of sun-dried mud bristling with wooden poles, in Djenné, in Mali. The second curves up at the corners like a temple roof, painted beams under clay tiles, in China. The third is stacked roof on roof, a tall wooden pyramid in Java. No dome on any of them, no pencil minaret. And all three are mosques, where people line up in rows and bow toward Mecca. How can three buildings look so unlike each other and do the same thing? Today: mosques of mud and wood.
screen: `A ROOF OF MUD IN MALI.` → `A TEMPLE ROOF IN CHINA.` → `A STACKED ROOF IN JAVA.`

segments.voice: The answer starts with a saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. In a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, he counts the things given to him, and one is this: the whole earth has been made a place of prayer for him and his community. Wherever the time of prayer finds you, you can pray there. So a mosque, at its simplest, is a clean place set apart, with the direction of Mecca marked. The rest is left to the builders, and builders use what they have. Second, the mud. We met Djenné earlier this year, the town that replasters its mosque together. This time, look at the method. In a land of river clay and heat, thick mud walls help keep a building cool, and the wooden poles give the plasterers a foothold when the walls are renewed. Local material, local work. Third, China. Some old Chinese mosques were built in the style of Chinese halls: courtyards, gates, timber, curved roofs, inscriptions in Arabic and Chinese side by side. A visitor might take one for a temple until the rows begin. Fourth, Java. Some old mosques there have tiered roofs on great wooden pillars, the way halls were raised on that island. People in Demak tell of one pillar pieced together from leftover wood chips by a saintly teacher. It's a story, not a record, but it shows how dearly the building is loved. The Qur'an says God made people "nations and tribes that ye may know one another." The mosques look like their nations. The rows inside look the same.

1039.title: Istiqlal and Sheikh Zayed
1039.hook: great modern mosques in Jakarta and Abu Dhabi
1039.howItsDone: Large modern mosques often host Friday prayer, Ramadan night prayers and Eid gatherings, and some, like Sheikh Zayed in Abu Dhabi, welcome visitors with guided tours.

segments.voice: Yesterday: mosques of mud and wood, in Djenné, in China and in Java. Your line was every land builds its own.

Jakarta, Friday, noon. Motorbikes thread between buses, and in the middle of it all stands a vast white mosque with a broad dome and a single tall minaret. Its name is one word: Istiqlal. Independence. Across the road rises a Catholic cathedral with tall, pointed spires. Now cross an ocean to Abu Dhabi: a mosque of white marble, domes like clustered pearls, flowers of colored stone set into the floors, and tour groups of every faith walking through in the late afternoon. Two mosques, both raised in living memory. Today: Istiqlal and Sheikh Zayed.
screen: `JAKARTA: A MOSQUE CALLED INDEPENDENCE.` → `A CATHEDRAL ACROSS THE ROAD.` → `ABU DHABI: WHITE MARBLE, OPEN DOORS.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Istiqlal is the Arabic word for independence, and the mosque was planned as the national mosque of a newly independent Indonesia. A country that had just won its freedom chose to say so with a house of prayer. Second, the architect. The chosen design came from Friedrich Silaban, an Indonesian architect who was a Christian. A Christian drew the plans for the national mosque, and it stands across from the cathedral. Some Indonesians point to that pair as a picture of neighbors living side by side. Third, Abu Dhabi. The Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque carries the name of the leader who founded the United Arab Emirates, and he is buried beside it. Its builders gathered marble, stone, glass and craftsmen from many countries, and its doors stay open to visitors of every faith, with guides to explain what they're seeing. Fourth, why build at all, when the whole earth is already a place of prayer? A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says that whoever builds a mosque, seeking the face of God, God builds for him a house like it in Paradise. And the Qur'an says who keeps a mosque alive. In Pickthall's translation: "He only shall tend Allah's sanctuaries who believeth in Allah and the Last Day." Marble and domes are one thing. Tending is another: the people who pray, sweep and teach there. The Ka'ba, Medina, Jerusalem, Djenné, Jakarta, Abu Dhabi: every one of them was once new, once built today.

1040.title: Your nearest mosque
1040.hook: every mosque is linked to the first
1040.howItsDone: Muslims pray in the nearest mosque when they can, especially for Friday prayer, facing the mihrab toward Mecca; some mosques also welcome visitors and hold open days.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Istiqlal in Jakarta, the mosque named independence, and Sheikh Zayed with its open doors. Your line was built today.

Somewhere near you there may well be a mosque. It might have a dome. It might be a converted shop with a hand-painted sign, a room above a pharmacy, a prayer space in a hospital basement or a university hallway. You may have walked past it without looking up. Inside, on the front wall, there's very likely a small arched niche, or just a mark, showing which way to face. That mark is a thread. Pull it, and it runs across roads, seas and deserts to one house in Mecca. Today, the last of our houses of prayer: your nearest mosque.
screen: `A DOME, A SHOP, A BASEMENT ROOM.` → `A NICHE ON THE FRONT WALL.` → `A THREAD TO MECCA.`

segments.voice: First, the thread. The niche is the mihrab, and the direction it shows is the qibla, toward the Ka'ba. The Qur'an tells believers that wherever they are, they turn their faces toward the Sacred Mosque in prayer. So the smallest prayer room and the grandest hall point the same way. Second, the first house. Five days ago we heard the Qur'an call the house at Becca "the first Sanctuary appointed for mankind." A shop-front prayer room in a city you've never seen is turned toward that same house: linked to the first. Third, the way in. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says whoever enters a mosque should pray two units of prayer before sitting down, a greeting for the house itself. Visitors who aren't Muslim aren't asked to pray, of course. Shoes come off at the door, people dress modestly, and a quiet hello goes a long way. Some mosques hold open days and welcome questions. Fourth, the blessing. Four days ago, in Medina, we heard the verse asking believers to send blessings on the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. Those blessings are called salawat, and some Muslims say them as they step into a mosque. Now look back. This long stretch walked through history and civilization: caliphs and scholars, libraries and soup kitchens, empires, colonial rule, migration, and these houses of prayer. Mecca, Medina, Jerusalem, mud and wood, Jakarta and Abu Dhabi, and the one down your street. Next comes a new camp: the holy days in history.

1041.title: Ramadan: the lanterns
1041.hook: Cairo's Ramadan lanterns, a custom centuries old
1041.howItsDone: In Egypt and in some families elsewhere, Ramadan lanterns are hung in streets, shop doorways and homes for the month, and children carry small ones in the evenings.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the houses of prayer with your nearest mosque, its mihrab pointing along the qibla to Mecca. Your line was linked to the first.

A Cairo alley, just after sunset, in the month of fasting. Strings of lights zigzag between balconies. In a shop doorway hang lanterns in rows: tin frames punched with patterns, panes of red, green and blue glass, a little door on the side for the candle. A child walks past swinging a small one, singing. Some newer ones are plastic and play a tune when you press a button. The old ones smell of hot metal and wax. The whole street glows like the inside of a jewel box. A new camp starts today, the holy days in history, and it opens with one object. Today's word: fanous.
screen: `A CAIRO ALLEY AFTER SUNSET.` → `TIN, COLORED GLASS, A CANDLE.` → `A NEW CAMP: THE HOLY DAYS.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Fanous is the Arabic word for a lantern, and in Egypt it has come to mean the Ramadan lantern above all. Second, the story. People in Cairo tell of a Fatimid ruler who arrived in the city by night; the people came out carrying lanterns to light his way, and the lanterns stayed with the month. Other versions put them in the hands of children, or of women walking out after dark in the fasting month. Nobody can prove which is true. What the stories agree on is light, and Ramadan nights. Third, why light belongs here. The Qur'an names the month itself: "The month of Ramadan in which was revealed the Qur'an, a guidance for mankind." And elsewhere it gives a picture made of light. In Pickthall's translation: "Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The similitude of His light is as a niche wherein is a lamp. The lamp is in a glass. The glass is as it were a shining star." A lamp, in a glass, in a niche. Some readers hear that verse in the glow of a fanous. Fourth, the street. Ramadan nights are busy: the meal at sunset, the night prayers, visits to family, a late walk. The fanous turns the dark street into a place to be. Far from Egypt, some families hang one by the door, or set one on the iftar table, so the children know the month has come.

segments.voice: Light a candle or a lamp, or simply look at the nearest glow, a screen dimmed low, a streetlight through the window, and watch where its edge meets the dark. Let your breathing slow until the light seems steady. If you pray, recall the verse of light, a lamp in a glass, in a niche; if not, just rest your eyes on the glow.
Fanous. The lantern, and in Egypt above all the Ramadan lantern of tin and colored glass, carried through the streets after sunset. Today's word.
Your line: lanterns for ramadan. A small light turns a dark street into a place to be. That's day one thousand forty-one.

1042.title: Ramadan: the iftar cannon
1042.hook: in some cities a cannon marks sunset for breaking the fast
1042.howItsDone: Muslims fasting in Ramadan break the fast at the call to the maghrib prayer, at sunset or, in Shia practice, a little after, often with dates and water; in some cities a cannon is fired at that moment.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the fanous, the Ramadan lantern of tin and colored glass. Your line was lanterns for ramadan.

Late afternoon in the fasting month. A table is laid: dates in a bowl, water in glasses, soup keeping warm, a plate nobody may touch yet. Children hover. Somebody checks the window; somebody else checks a phone. Everyone is listening. Then, from the hill across the city, a deep boom rolls over the rooftops, and the whole house moves at once. A date. A sip of water. Someone laughs. In some cities, that boom is the sound of sunset in Ramadan. Today: the iftar cannon.
screen: `DATES, WATER, AND WAITING.` → `A BOOM FROM THE HILL.` → `THE WHOLE HOUSE MOVES AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: First, what the cannon answers. The Qur'an sets the edges of the fasting day: eat and drink until the dawn is clear, and then, in Pickthall's translation, "Then strictly observe the fast till nightfall." In Sunni practice the fast ends at sunset, with the call to the sunset prayer; in Shia practice, a little later, when the redness has left the eastern sky. Before clocks on every wrist, a whole city needed to know the same moment. A call from a minaret carries only so far; a cannon carries much farther. Second, the story. People in Cairo tell it in several versions: a ruler was testing a new cannon, and by chance it fired just at sunset in Ramadan. The people took it as a signal and thanked him, and the firing became a custom. Whether it happened that way, nobody can say. But the custom spread, and in some cities a cannon still fires at sunset in Ramadan, sometimes carried on television and radio. Third, the hurry. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says people will remain in good as long as they hurry to break the fast. Not lingering, not proving how long you can last. The Qur'an gives the fast a firm edge at both ends, and the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, asked people not to blur the second. Fourth, the joy. Another hadith says the one who fasts has two joys: one when breaking the fast, and one on meeting the Lord. The cannon is the sound of the first joy, heard by a whole city at once.

1043.title: Ramadan: the drummer
1043.hook: a drummer walks the streets before dawn to wake people for suhur
1043.howItsDone: In parts of Egypt and other Muslim-majority lands, a musaharati still walks the streets before dawn in Ramadan with a small drum, calling households by name to wake for suhur.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the iftar cannon, one boom to tell a whole city the fast is over. Your line was the cannon at sunset.

Tap. Tap-tap. Tap. It's the dark hour before dawn in a Ramadan street, and the only sound is a small drum. A man walks under the balconies with a lantern and a stick, striking a little drum slung at his side. He stops at a door and calls a name. Not a general shout: a name. The son of the baker. The widow on the second floor. Upstairs, a light goes on. Then another. A child at a window waves, and he waves back without missing a beat. Today's word is what people call him: musaharati.
screen: `A DRUM BEFORE DAWN.` → `HE CALLS YOU BY NAME.` → `ONE LIGHT, THEN ANOTHER.`

segments.voice: First, the job. The musaharati, as he's called in Egypt, wakes people for suhur, the meal eaten in the dark before the fast begins at dawn. Other places have other names for the same work. Second, the chant. As he walks, he calls out lines inviting the sleeper to wake and to declare God one, and then he adds the names of the households. That's the heart of it: a whole street, known by name, woken one door at a time. Third, a waking call in Medina. Hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari tell that in the Prophet's own city, peace be upon him, Bilal used to call out while it was still night, so that sleepers would wake. The Prophet told the people that Bilal's call did not mean the fast had begun: keep eating and drinking until Ibn Umm Maktum calls, for he calls at dawn. Two voices, one to wake, one to mark the start. Fourth, the gentleness. Nobody wants to be shaken awake. The musaharati comes with rhythm, a lantern and your own name, and he's gone before you're cross. Alarms and phones often do the job now, yet in some neighborhoods the drummer still walks, and children still wait at the window for him. Look back at this week: the farthest mosque in Jerusalem; mosques of mud and wood; mosques built today; your nearest mosque and its qibla; then Ramadan, with its lanterns, its cannon, and now its drummer. Places, then nights.
screen: `HE WAKES THE STREET FOR SUHUR.` · `WAKE, SLEEPER, AND DECLARE GOD ONE.` · `BILAL CALLS BY NIGHT.` · `A RHYTHM, A LANTERN, YOUR NAME.` · then, large: `WAKE FOR SUHUR.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you'll speak to first tomorrow, a child, a partner, a parent, a roommate, and how you usually reach them: a shout up the stairs, a text. Now picture doing it the drummer's way: a soft knock, their name said kindly, a little patience while they come round. If you pray, hold that person in your prayer; if not, simply wish them a good morning before it comes.
Musaharati. The Ramadan drummer who walks the streets before dawn, calling each house by name to wake for suhur. Today's word.
